sources.name: Prompt Caching: Cut Your AI Cost by 90% (already in corpus)
Kevin Weil — OpenAI CPO on model maximalism (already in corpus)

cards.back: Instructing the model to reason step-by-step before giving a final answer rather than jumping straight to it — generating intermediate reasoning tokens measurably improves accuracy on multi-step problems, especially math and logic.

cards.front: Why do system prompts matter more than user-turn instructions for consistent behavior?
cards.back: The system prompt sets persistent context, persona, and constraints that apply across the entire conversation, while user turns are one-off requests. Putting stable rules (tone, format, boundaries) in the system prompt keeps behavior consistent even as users phrase requests differently turn to turn.

cards.front: What is few-shot prompting, and when does it help most?
cards.back: Providing 2-5 example input/output pairs in the prompt before the real request — most useful when the desired output format or style is unusual or hard to describe in words alone; the examples do the specifying that instructions can't.

cards.front: What is structured output (e.g. forced JSON) and why does it matter for production systems?
cards.back: Constraining the model's output to a specific schema rather than free text. Critical for production because downstream code needs to parse the response reliably — free text requires fragile regex/parsing that breaks on format drift.

cards.front: Why is "tool calling" considered a prompt-engineering skill, not just an API feature?
cards.back: How you name and describe a tool — its parameters, when to use it vs. not — directly determines whether the model calls it correctly and at the right moment. A poorly described tool gets misused or ignored regardless of how good the underlying function is; the tool description IS a prompt.

cards.front: When should you use XML-style tags to structure a prompt versus plain prose?
cards.back: When a prompt has multiple distinct sections the model needs to treat differently (e.g. <context>, <instructions>, <examples>) — tags give the model unambiguous boundaries, reducing the chance it conflates instructions with reference material, especially in long prompts.

cards.front: What is prompt caching, and what's the practical benefit?
cards.back: Marking a portion of the prompt — a long system prompt or document — as reusable across calls so the model doesn't reprocess it from scratch each time. Cuts both cost and latency significantly for repeated or similar requests.

cards.front: Why does "put it in context" usually beat "hope the model remembers it" for anything important?
cards.back: The context window is the model's working memory — directly accessible and precise. Parametric/trained-in knowledge is more like vague recollection, prone to blending facts or hallucinating specifics. If a fact matters, include it explicitly rather than trusting recall.

cards.front: What's the difference between zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuned approaches to getting a specific model behavior?
cards.back: Zero-shot: instructions only, fastest to try, least reliable for unusual formats. Few-shot: instructions plus examples, better format-fidelity, costs context tokens every call. Fine-tuned: the behavior is baked into the weights — most reliable and cheapest per-call at scale, but requires training data and infrastructure.

cards.front: Why does "model maximalism" change how you should prompt-engineer today?
cards.back: Building elaborate prompt scaffolding to work around a model's current weaknesses is a bet that pays off short-term but gets obsoleted as the model improves every 2-3 months — the scaffolding becomes dead weight. Design for where the model is heading, not just where it is today.
